# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 1 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 1 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_001_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 1, Chapter 1

**1** The man who raised me sold me to a certain Rhoda in Rome. After many years I came to know her again, and I came to love her as a sister. **2** Some time later I saw her bathing in the Tiber River, and I reached out my hand and helped her out of the river. Seeing her beauty, I reasoned within my heart, saying: "How happy I would be if I had a wife of such beauty and character." That was all I thought — nothing more. **3** After some time had passed, as I was walking to Cumae and praising the creations of God — how great and marvelous and powerful they are — I fell asleep as I walked. **4** And the Spirit carried me off through a trackless region, through which no man could pass — the place was rugged and cut through by water channels. **5** Crossing that river, I came to level ground, and I knelt and began to pray to the Lord and confess my sins. **6** While I was praying, the heavens opened, and I saw the woman I had desired greeting me from heaven: "Greetings, Hermas." **7** I looked up at her and said, "Lady, what are you doing here?" She answered, "I was taken up in order to expose your sins before the Lord." **8** I said to her, "Are you now my accuser?" "No," she said, "but hear the words I am about to speak to you. God, who dwells in the heavens and created all things out of nothing, and multiplied and increased them for the sake of his holy church — **9** he is angry with you because you sinned against me." I answered her: "How did I sin against you? When did I ever speak a dishonorable word to you? Did I not always treat you like a goddess? Did I not always honor you as a sister? Why do you falsely accuse me, woman, of these wicked and unclean things?" **10** She laughed and said to me, "The desire for wickedness arose in your heart. Or does it not seem to you to be sin for a righteous man to have an evil desire arise in his heart? Yes, it is sin," she said, "and a great one at that. For the righteous man aims at righteous things. **11** As long as he aims at righteous things and walks in them, he has a Lord in the heavens. But those who aim at wicked things and live accordingly have a lord who is wicked, ruinous, and destructive. And those caught between them come to ruin. **12** For when people who are holy and just allow evil desires to arise, they bring sin upon themselves."

---

### Council Notes

This opening chapter establishes the biographical frame: Hermas as freedman, Rhoda as his former owner turned heavenly witness. The "sin" is entirely internal — a fleeting desire, never acted upon — yet treated as genuinely culpable. This is a remarkable moral psychology.

The identity of the heavenly woman is initially left open; she is later revealed to be the personified Church (ch 3). Her laughter in v. 10 is startling — divine figures rarely laugh in apocalyptic literature.

The theology of creation ex nihilo (v. 8: "who created things out of that which is not") is an early and explicit attestation of this doctrine.
